sources.title: How to Use Pandas in Python

steps.title: Install pandas and prepare dataset
steps.instructions: Install pandas with pip install pandas (or uv add pandas). Put orders.csv from the tutorial repository in your project folder.

targets.caption: Install pandas in the project terminal

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip or pip3
Setting up a virtual environment with uv

hints: Open the integrated terminal inside VS Code or Cursor.
Run pip install pandas on Windows, pip3 install pandas on Mac/Linux, or uv init . followed by uv add pandas.
Ensure orders.csv is saved in the root of your project directory.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on macOS or Linux.
Installing pandas in a uv virtual environment and then running python directly instead of uv run.

steps.title: Load and print CSV in Python
steps.instructions: In main.py, import pandas as pd, load orders.csv into df with pd.read_csv and print(df). Run the script and check the table prints.

explanations.topic: Aliasing pandas as pd
DataFrame and Series core types
Structure of the orders.csv dataset

hints: Start main.py with import pandas as pd.
Call pd.read_csv("orders.csv"), store it in df, and pass df to print().
Run python main.py (or uv run .\main.py) in the terminal.
common_mistakes: Running the command from outside the folder containing orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Forgetting quotes around orders.csv inside pd.read_csv().
steps.code: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"); print(df)

steps.title: Create notebook and load CSV
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb, import pandas and load orders.csv in the first cell, then print(df) in a second cell.

explanations.topic: Creating and saving a Jupyter notebook
Running independent notebook cells

hints: Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P) and choose Create: New Jupyter Notebook, then save as notebook.ipynb.
Put import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in the first cell and run it.
Add a second code cell with print(df) and execute it.
common_mistakes: Running the print(df) cell before executing the cell that defines df.
Missing the Python extension in VS Code or Cursor required to run notebook cells.
steps.code: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

steps.title: Inspect DataFrame structure and stats
steps.instructions: Explore the DataFrame with df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index in notebook cells.

targets.caption: Inspect column types and entry counts

explanations.topic: Previewing first and last rows with head and tail
Viewing types and statistics with info and describe
Inspecting column labels and row index

hints: Run df.head() and df.tail() to preview the top 5 and bottom 5 rows.
Run df.info() for column types and df.describe() for summary statistics.
Evaluate df.columns and df.index without parentheses.
common_mistakes: Adding parentheses to df.columns or df.index, which are properties rather than methods.
Omitting parentheses on df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), or df.describe().
steps.code: df.head(); df.tail(); df.info(); df.describe(); df.columns; df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows with iloc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, select one column as a Series and several columns as a DataFrame with brackets, then read specific rows and cells with df.iloc.

targets.caption: Retrieve a single row by integer index position

explanations.topic: Selecting one column returns a Series
Selecting a list of columns returns a DataFrame
Indexing rows and cells with df.iloc

hints: Use df["Country"] for a single column or pass a list like df[["Country", "Product"]] for multiple columns.
Use df.iloc[10] to get the row at integer index 10.
Chain a column name such as df.iloc[10]["Shipped"] to inspect one field.
common_mistakes: Using single brackets df["Country", "Product"] instead of double brackets for multiple columns.
Trying df[0] instead of df.iloc[0] to index a row by integer position.

steps.title: Filter DataFrame rows with conditions
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, filter rows with comparison conditions combined with & and |, string methods (.str.startswith/.endswith), and .isin() with ~ negation.

targets.caption: Filter rows whose column value matches a list

explanations.topic: Combining filters with & and |
Filtering text columns with .str methods
Matching lists with .isin and inverting with ~

hints: Wrap each condition in parentheses when combining filters with & (and) or | (or).
Use df[df["CustomerName"].str.startswith("A")] or .str.endswith("a") for text matching.
Use .isin([...]) to match any value in a list and ~ in front of the condition to negate it.
common_mistakes: Using Python's and/or keywords instead of & and | between Series conditions.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |.

steps.title: Update values and drop rows
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, use df.loc to update matching rows and .str.upper() to uppercase a column, then delete a row with df.drop().

targets.caption: Locate matching rows by label/condition and assign new values

explanations.topic: Conditional row and column updates with df.loc
Transforming all values in a column
Removing rows by index with df.drop

hints: Pass the row filter and target column name to df.loc[condition, "Column"] = new_value.
Assign df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper() to convert all countries to uppercase.
Reassign df = df.drop(39) to remove row 39 from the DataFrame.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning back to df, leaving df unchanged.
Using == instead of = for the assignment on the right side of df.loc.
steps.code: df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"; df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper(); df = df.drop(39)

steps.title: Clean missing values and rename columns
steps.instructions: Handle missing values with df.dropna() / df.fillna(), and rename a column with df.rename(columns=...).

explanations.topic: Dropping or filling missing values with dropna and fillna
Modifying a DataFrame directly with inplace=True
Renaming column headers with df.rename

hints: Use df.dropna() to drop rows with null values or df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True) to fill them.
Pass columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"} and inplace=True to df.rename().
Run df in a new cell to confirm the Order ID column header updated.
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True or reassignment when calling fillna() or rename().
Passing a list instead of a {old: new} dictionary to columns= in df.rename().
steps.code: df.dropna(); df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True); df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)

steps.title: Group, sort, and export CSV
steps.instructions: Analyze with value_counts(), groupby(...).sum() and sort_values(..., ascending=False), then export with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).

explanations.topic: Counting unique values with value_counts
Grouping and summing values with groupby
Sorting rows and exporting CSV without index

hints: Call df["Country"].value_counts() and df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum() to summarize by country.
Use df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False) to sort from highest price to lowest.
Export with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False) so row indices are excluded.
common_mistakes: Omitting index=False in to_csv(), which adds an extra index column to the CSV.
Omitting ascending=False in sort_values() when descending order is wanted.
steps.code: df["Country"].value_counts(); df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum(); df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False); df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)
